articles.text: The City of Piedmont has reached an agreement with East Bay Community Energy (EBCE) to install four single-port fast Electric Vehicle (EV) charging stations on Magnolia Avenue near the Exedra Plaza. The City Council approved the appropriation of $75,000 from the General Fund to facilitate the costs at an October 18 meeting. This approved location is a shift from the proposed four charging stations next to the Rec. Tennis courts on Bonita Avenue as discussed by City Council on June 21. The original proposed 10-year agreement would have allowed EBCE to install two dual-port, fast-charging stations at the location, which would be able to charge up to four vehicles at one time. Council members discussed whether the location was appropriate and whether the one-hour charging limit could be extended but delayed a vote. The council delayed a vote again on July 19. Special Assistant to City Administrator Paul Benoit told council members that staff had requested to pull the agenda item and return to city council for consideration. “Progress is being made with East Bay Community Energy in addressing the concerns that council expressed in the past. Our preference is to bring a fully-baked plan that we feel is going as far as we can go with East Bay Energy, but it’s just not ready yet,” Benoit said on July 19. The plan presented to council at its October 18 meeting was approved unanimously. “Other than the location and increased time allotment [to charge] from 60 minutes to 90 minutes, the terms of agreement were unchanged from June,” confirmed City Administrator Sara Lillevand. articles.text: An all-day meeting on Tuesday, November 2 by an advisory panel of medical and public health experts at the Center for Disease Control (CDC) resulted in unanimous agreement to approve BioNTech and Pfizer Inc.’s COVID-19 vaccine for children aged 5-11. Within hours, the CDC director Dr. Rochelle Walensky, gave final approval, and kids in the U.S. can start receiving the vaccine today, Wednesday November 3. Piedmont School District vaccine policy requires parents to provide the district with proof of their child’s vaccination within eight weeks of emergency approval. As of press time the district had not announced an official date for 5-11 year olds to provide proof of full vaccination. The district was one of the first in the nation to mandate the vaccine for students 12 and up on September 22, and also led the way with a mandate for teachers on October 17. Weekly testing and statements of personal or religious belief against the vaccine are not valid alternatives for teachers or students. Only doctors’ notes will be considered. There is some wiggle room once the district sets a start date for the eight week period if vaccine rollout proves to be difficult. “If supply of the vaccine in the Bay Area becomes an issue, the Policy also gives the Superintendent authority to adjust the deadline as necessary,” said PUSD’s Director of Communications Brian Killgore. articles.text: The following letter was sent to the Piedmont Public Works Department and City Council. Editor: My neighborhood at Rose and Linda Aves and the streets surrounding Beach School have lots of beautiful street trees. Every year in this season, they drop their leaves. Every year the City sends its very expensive street sweeping vehicle to clean the gutters and keep the leaves out of our storm drains. This year, like in years past, only about 1/3 of the gutters are cleaned. Why? Because cars are parked on street-cleaning day. They fill the streets for two reasons: 1) There are no signs saying No Parking on street cleaning mornings 2) There is no enforcement of the No Parking advisory. Sometimes a resident will voluntarily post signs in front of his house, and once in a while a police officer will ticket offending parkers. They seem to do that only if: 1) The resident calls the City 72 hours in advance 2) The resident calls the City on street cleaning day to report a violation 3) A police dispatcher determines that proper 72-hours notice was given. This so-called “parking enforcement” only applies to the residence of the active volunteer. As a result of this overburdened, ridiculous process, the City’s expensive street sweeping vehicle wastes fuel and depreciation costs by just driving around, not sweeping, because of cars parked where the leaves have accumulated. This can easily be solved. 1) The City should post permanent signs identifying the No Parking days. 2) The City should police the scheduled streets on sweeping days and enforce the No Parking signs. 3) The street sweeping vehicle driver should call into headquarters to report the location of offending vehicles. With all due respect, please implement a responsible, systematic policy for assuring that our streets are cleaned and city resources are used effectively. articles.text: The City of Piedmont and ELS Architecture and Urban Design kicked off a series of community workshops on Tuesday, November 2. ELS was chosen by the city council to design a new Piedmont Community Pool complex. Two sessions were held on Tuesday – in the early afternoon and evening – allowing residents to learn about the process that the firm and city will use over the next three years. ELS staff were available to answer questions about programming potential, project size and scope, budget, and timeline. The new pool is slated to open in 2-1/2 years, in summer 2024. The first workshop served as an opportunity for residents to share thoughts and aspirations about the project. It also marked an opportunity for the firm to gather information from Piedmonters to refine the final design Clarence Mamuyac, principal at ELS Architects, describes plans for public meetings to discuss the city’s new aquatic complex. Residents gather for the first community workshop about the planned new pool. The gathering was held in the Veterans Hall yesterday at 1 p.m. concept. Project goals include, at minimum, two pools and a twostory support building envisioned in the 2016 conceptual plan. ELS and the City is targeting winter 2022 for design concept completion - that is also the target date for construction to begin. “We need more information, more input, that’s what this [first workshop] is about,” said Clarence Mamuyac, the design firm’s principal architect. “We’ll gather information from this session, and then on November 16, we will present ideas and will deputize everyone who shows up that day as architects. [Residents] will help us critique those ideas.” Mamuyac told the crowd that, at the final scheduled workshop, December 14, the preferred direction will be presented. “Let me say at the onset, it’s not going to satisfy everybody,” he told the audience. “But we will hear you, we will try our best to come up with solutions that fit most needs.” ELS will move forward with developing a draft program and concept directions for presentation, comment, and critique from the public. The next workshop is on Tuesday, November 16, from 7 p.m. to 8:30 p.m. Following the presentation, attendees will be invited to join a design team for a 20-minute charrette.
articles.title: Community workshop for new pool hosted by ELS and city on Nov. 2

articles.text: The League of Women Voters Piedmont will host a town hall tomorrow, November 4, at 4 p.m. to discuss the new Piedmont Pool. Audience members are invited to ask Project Manager George Sanen questions about the process thus far. The virtual town hall will highlight Piedmont’s plans for the new community pool. In November 2020, voters approved $19.5 million in general obligation bonds to finance a new pool that will replace the aging aquatic facility. The current pool closed indefinitely on September 8, 2020; the new community pool is set to be completed in summer 2024. This event will include brief presentations from the city’s team which will be followed by an audience question-and-answer segment moderated by League of Women Voters Piedmont President Lorrel Plimier. Guest speakers are Sanen, Special Assistant to the City Administrator Paul Benoit, and City Administrator Sara Lillevand. Register for free at lwvpiedmont.org/events to receive an email with the Zoom link information. This program will be recorded, and you can watch it live or at a later date on the League of Women Voters Piedmont YouTube channel.

articles.text: Let your kids play in the rain. As a Californian we all know how important rain (and snow) are to our very existence. It is something we need in order for trees to grow, crops yield, and to make sure water flows freely from the tap. We take these things for granted until they are limited. and then we value them. As a proponent of outdoor play and its importance to the growth of children’s bodies and brains, I am doubly supportive of playing outdoors in the rain. Rain gives children an opportunity to engage in a different type of play – especially in California where rain is inconsistent, at best. What a treat it is to play outside in the rain. For children there are many benefits for this change up in outdoor adventure: • Shift in the senses Everything is different when it’s raining. The dimension of sight, smell, touch and sound are all changed when it’s raining. Exploring the outdoors in the rain gives children an opportunity to try out their motor skills in a different environment. A wet and slippery world is very different (and fun). Taking a rain walk and observing together the shift in all the senses is an exploration worth taking. • Boost in creativity The rainy landscape brings the world into a new view. Sand and mud turn into molding clay, surfaces are slippery – sometimes dangerous, sometimes fun. All of this changes the normal outdoor play spots into spaces where imaginations can run free. Playing in what was a grassy field might now be a lake with a sea serpent. • Staying Active the family outdoor experience, we expand the opportunity to get kids moving. Keeping kids active means less adverse health outcomes over time. It may be messy, but it is fun. • Navigating Nature Playing outdoors is of course important for many reasons, but embracing the outdoors in all weather, including rainy, wet days helps children deepen their connection with nature, perhaps creating lifelong attitudes and behaviors. Winter is coming. I feel like there may be rain in the forecast. Get your raincoat and boots and have an adventure on a rainy day. Kymberly Miller is the Executive Director of Children’s Fairyland, the mission of which is to spark imagination, learning, and development through the power of storytelling.

We are co-chairing the Giving Campaign this year because we want to ensure Piedmont schools continue to provide an excellent education for all of our children. Between our two families, we have five children who attend the Piedmont schools at all levels, from elementary to high school. The past year and a half have been rough for all of us, but we are so happy that the kids are back in school and re-engaging with their teachers, their fellow students, and their activities. PUSD has done a great job re-opening our schools this fall and they need our support more than ever. During the pandemic, like everyone we know, we thought about our options. After careful consideration, we recommitted to the Piedmont schools. They offer a well-rounded, comprehensive curriculum in a safe, welcoming, community-oriented environment. The Piedmont teachers and staff are dedicated to ensuring that every child has the opportunity to thrive. In order to help our schools and our students succeed, we need to support them financially. The reality is that our government does not provide sufficient funds for our public schools. The premiere of Louis-Vuitton Foundation’s The Morozov Collection: Icons of Modern Art culls 200 works from their lifetime collections. The exhibition is the logical sequel to The Shchukin Collection: Icons of Modern Art of 2017, where Morozov colleague Sergei Shchukin’s reputation was rehabilitated as a trailblazer when he was bringing Paris art to Moscow. The Morozov and Shchukin families both inherited their fortunes from textiles. The families were close, but rivals, competing to buy from the same Paris art dealers. Shchukin created a benevolent pathway to bring art to the Russian public, filling the walls of his palatial home with nouveau art that stunned and excited the senses, created controversy and debate. Many of Shchukin’s contemporaries were in awe at the notion of public art, as Russia had none. The Morozov brothers were like-minded, and welcomed the public. The third generation Morozov sons, Mikhail and Ivan. were born into a rarefied life where they devotedly pursued the arts, unlike Shchukin who didn’t begin collecting art until age 40. The Morozov brothers also benefitted from a much broader education than Shchukin, and as teenagers they entered apprenticeships with influential Russian painters Valentin Serov and Konstantin Korovin, family-portrait painters already ensconced in the varying Morozov households. Her sons learned to paint plein air, developing an adoration of landscapes. Varvara was the industrialist in the family, a Morozov textile heiress alongside her five brothers, each a participant in the Morozov empire. Mikhail graduated in history and linguistics and wrote a comedy for the stage. Ivan painted well as a hobby, and he was sent to Zurich to study chemistry and learn new dye techniques; but both men preferred the arts to managing the factories they inherited. He too traveled to Paris, often buying from his brother’s preferred art dealers, Ambroise Vollard and Paul Durand-Ruel. Ivan Morozov proved to be an eager buyer, acquiring Picasso’s Two Acrobats, Renoir’s La Rêverie, and Monet’s A Corner of the Garden at Montgeron. articles.text: Highlanders upset #1 Berkeley 12-8; beat Alameda 6-5 in semifinals A the scorekeeper’s clock struck zero at poolside, Piedmont water polo coach John Savage shot his arms above his head, screaming exuberantly. His team had just defeated Berkeley 12-8 to win the championship of the Western Alameda County Conference for the first time. The victory last Saturday, October 30 at the Encinal pool in Alameda, was Piedmont’s first league title after getting close a number of times in the past __ years. “I’ve been coaching for nine years and played for four years when at the school before college. I don’t think we’ve ever won, I know it hasn’t happened in my time,” Savage said. “The boys did an incredible job. It was a whole team effort; every single person on this team played a role. I am incredibly proud of them.” Savage helped lead the school to third-place finishes in 2021 and 2019, and his teams were in the finals in 2018 and 2014. Piedmont entered the WACC Tournament this fall as the No. 3 seeded team, but upset No. 2 Alameda 6-5 in the semifinals on Thursday, October 28. Berkeley entered as the two-time defending champions. Notably, Piedmont’s accomplishment was done without any superstars. In prior years it benefitted from the skill of Max Wagener, now at the University of Redlands, Henry Saunders, now at USC, Patrick Conn, currently playing for the University of Toronto. “This is a very complete team. Staff Photos Goalie Dariush Kashani makes a monumental save on a penalty shot by Alameda in the semifinals. Antonio Rivera scored five goals against Berkeley and two in the finals against Alameda, including the game-winner. Piedmont coach John Savage (right) celebrates his water polo team’s first league title. I can trust anyone in the water with the ball,” said Savage. “They knew what they are doing, and they can attack, attack, attack. Today, our defense was set up to attack Berkeley’s best player, Chase [McFarland], an incredible athlete,” “In my freshman year, we had a really good squad with Patrick and Henry, and they really set the foundation for us to compete year-in and year-out,” added senior captain Antonio Rivera. “We’ve kept that legacy going by setting a new high. We’ve had a lot of close games where our defense has had to stick it out, and that’s what happened these last two games. We’ve stuck with the system and its working,” The Yellowjackets entered the match after defeating Bishop O’Dowd 25-22 in the semifinals, not exactly a defensive showcase. Piedmont won a tight 6-5 victory in the other semifinal against Alameda. articles.text: The Head of The Charles Regatta crosses under six historic bridges on the Charles River, and historically attracts hundreds of thousands of spectators from all over the world. The Oakland Strokes returned to the prestigious Head of the Charles Regatta in Cambridge, Massachusetts the weekend of October 22-24. Piedmont High senior Max Cole was in the Strokes’ varsity 8 boat, which 11th of 80 boats. Also competing from Piedmont High was senior Amelie Tristram in the Strokes’ Varsity 4 boat. The Head of The Charles is among the largest rowing events in the U.S. for youth and collegiate rowers, annually attracting hundreds of teams from around the world. Cole characterized the event as a moment he’s been waiting for since reading about the Head of the Charles when he was a freshman. “When the Head of The Charles came around, it was wild. There are an estimated 250,000 spectators; miles of tents everywhere selling and promoting products, college teams, all sorts of stuff. This is one of the biggest races in the world, Olympians have raced here,” said Cole, a PHS senior. “It’s well over 1,000 boats with races over three days, its nonstop. The bridges over the Charles River are crowded with people and even on the sides of the river, there are people everywhere. It really hit me on race day that I was about to compete in this event I’ve been dreaming about since my freshman year,” he added. The event was canceled in 2020 due to the global pandemic. Crew, as a whole, sustained a troublesome year and a half that featured little to no racing for some student-athletes. It made this year’s Head of Charles that much more special. “Last year, we weren’t allowed to practice in groups of more than eight, and mostly did singles… The last serious race before this was February of my sophomore year. You step out of the plane to Boston and it dawns on you, ‘Holy cow, I’m racing in one of the most prestigious races ever,’” said Cole. “The Charles is a very windy river. The coxes who steer the boat are very competitive and won’t yield if you’re going faster than them, so a boat actually crashed into us and forced us into a wide turn. Maybe we would’ve gained a few spots if that hadn’t happened, but I’m still happy with how we raced,” said Cole. Also competing from Piedmont were Ryan Tripp who helped Dartmouth finish fourth in the Men’s Lightweight Eight, and Andrew Stoddard, now at MIT.

Piedmont rowers compete at Head of The Charles Regatta By Jonathan Comeaux The Oakland Strokes returned to the prestigious Head of the Charles Regatta in Cambridge, Massachusetts the weekend of October 22-24. Piedmont High senior Max Cole was in the Strokes’ varsity 8 boat, which 11th of 80 boats. Also competing from Piedmont High was senior Amelie Tristram in the Strokes’ Varsity 4 boat. The Head of The Charles is among the largest rowing events in the U.S. for youth and collegiate rowers, annually attracting hundreds of teams from around the world. Cole characterized the event as a moment he’s been waiting for since reading about the Head of the Charles when he was a freshman. “When the Head of The Charles came around, it was wild. There are an estimated 250,000 spectators; miles of tents everywhere selling and promoting products, college teams, all sorts of stuff. This is one of the biggest races in the world, Olympians have raced here,” said Cole, a PHS senior. “It’s well over 1,000 boats with races over three days, its nonstop. The bridges over the Charles River are crowded with people and even on the sides of the river, there are people everywhere. It really hit me on race day that I was about to compete in this event I’ve been dreaming about since my freshman year,” he added. The event was canceled in 2020 due to the global pandemic. Crew, as a whole, sustained a troublesome year and a half that featured little to no racing for some student-athletes. It made this year’s Head of Charles that much more special. “Last year, we weren’t allowed to practice in groups of more than eight, and mostly did singles… The last serious race before this was February of my sophomore year. articles.text: Photos by Ernie Tai Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir Founder Susie Rahl (left), founding Artistic Director Bob Geary, Executive Director Keri Butkevich, and Artistic Director Eric Tuan. One hundred fifty supporters of the Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir gathered on Saturday evening, October 30, for the 2021 Benefit & Concert, “Harvest Moon Rising” (also known as the Singing Moon). Held outside on the lush grounds of the Oakland Museum of California, it was the first opportunity in almost two years for Choir parents and patrons to see one another, have an al fresco dinner, and enjoy choral music. The two choirs that performed – Ancora and Ensemble – last sang in person in January 2020, so the evening was a true homecoming. Strict COVID-19 measures were followed – all attendees were asked to access the Clear to Go! App, upload their vaccination cards (or a negative test), and answer a few questions. Those who were cleared received a QR code to show the event organizers on arrival. We were directed to wear our masks whenever we weren’t eating or drinking. And, eat and drink we did. The Benefit started with passed hors d’oeuvres as everyone was arriving, followed by a bountiful dinner buffet. For this writer there was some anxiety in the proximity of everyone again, but everyone observed the masks-on request. We were welcomed by the Choir’s Executive Director Keri Butkevich, Board of Directors President Poppea Dorsam, Benefit Co-Chair Roshmi Mukherji, Artistic Director Eric Tuan, and Benefit Sponsor Paul Swenson (who read a heartfelt poem he’d written when his daughter Lucy graduated from the Choir). The coming season will be the Choir’s 40th. It wouldn’t be a Benefit without choir performances. Two advanced choirs sang, Ancora and Ensemble. Ancora started with Cancion de Otono (Autumn Song) “Where do you come from, my love, And then where are you going? Return to the place where you came from, Keep going to where you are heading, my love.” They ended the set with Deep River, the popular spiritual from the early 20th century: “Oh, don’t you want to go to that Gospel-feast? That Promised Land, where all is peace? A live auction followed. Enthusiastic auctioneer Sharon Mor coaxed higher-and-higher bids from the audience, starting with an original choral composition by Artistic Director Eric Tuan, then two dinners hosted by James Bell and Foster Goldstrom. As night was falling, we used our phone’s flashlight to illuminate our raised bidding paddles. Ensemble followed, regaling us with Oscar Peterson’s Hymn to Freedom: “When every one joins in our song And together singing harmony That’s when we’ll be free.” The group ended with Bolo Bolo Sab Mil Bolo, a Hindu devotional: “Let us all chant together He carries a trident And sounds the drum. Let us all beat drums.” A second round of fund-raising, Fund A Need, will provide needed funding, including underwriting a choir at a Title 1 school. It appeared that virtually every attendee donated some amount, starting at $10,000 and going to $50. The last round was spirited with the “Last Man Standing” receiving a classical guitar emblazoned with artwork by choir members. It was both a fun and a productive evening, and literally a breath of fresh air as we all start to get back to normal. Ernie Tai is a PEBCC alumni parent, a former board member, and a super fan. articles.text: Photo by David Schroeder Mezzo-soprano Nikola Printz will sing the lead role as Dido in Opera San Jose’s production of Dido and Aeneas. Opera San Jose returns to live performances with Henry Purcell’s Dido and Aeneas at the California Theatre beginning November 13. Dido and Aeneas is an opera in a prologue and three acts, with a libretto by Nahum Tate. The production is directed by Joseph Marcheso, and features mezzo-soprano Nikola Printz as Dido and baritone Efrain Solis as Aeneas. Soprano Maya Kherani stars as Belina and award winning bass-baritone Nathan Stark is the Sorcerer. Running time is 60 minutes with no intermission. The season launched with a streaming production of Rimsky-Korsakov’s Mozart and Salieri. Dido and Aeneas will be followed by productions of Bizet’s Carmen in February, and Bernstein’s West Side Story in April. “This season we explore the necessity of human connection. We explore love and love interrupted. We witness people who are confronted by a world incompatible with who they are or who they wish to be,” General Director Khori Dastoor said in describing the company’s 2021- 22 season. Proof of vaccination is required to attend this event, and masks are required for all attendees at the California Theatre. Evening performances will begin at 7:30 p.m., and matinees will be at 2 p.m. For more information on COVID protocols and to obtain tickets to upcoming live performances, visit https://www. operasj.org/subscriptions/.

articles.text: 2021-22 season dedicated to the late Michael Morgan O a k l a n d S y m p h o n y announced that its 2021-2022 concert season will be dedicated to its late conductor and artistic director, Michael Morgan. Morgan served as Oakland Symphony’s Music Director and Conductor for more than 30 years before he passed away on August 20, 2021. “It would be very hard to overstate the impact that Michael Morgan has had on not only the Oakland Symphony, but the entire Orchestra field,” said James Hasler, President of the Oakland Symphony Board of Trustees. “For more than 30 years he championed the role of the Oakland Symphony as a community builder – bringing us all together through dedication to education, celebration of the full range of music in our community, and leadership in collaborating with other local arts organizations. We miss him very much and we will find comfort in his spirit that will be with us forever.” The memorial season runs performing Florence Price Piano Concerto. The program also includes William Grant Still’s The Colored Soldiers Who Died for Democracy, and Beethoven’s Symphony No. 3 (Eroica). As an added feature, a pre-concert talk from the stage will be given by John Kendall Bailey at 7:05 p.m. “Our season is presenting guest conductors who were connected to Michael as colleagues, as those he influenced, and those who influenced him,” said Symphony Executive Director Mieko Hatano. “In accepting the engagement, each spoke to the singular values of the Oakland Symphony as an orchestra that is recognized nationally as an authentic voice of social justice through music. These conductors all built their Oakland Symphony programs upon those values. We look forward to welcoming each of them on the podium during our Memorial Season.” To purchase tickets for the November 19 concert, and for more information, visit www. articles.text: HG Wells’ The Time Machine is a magical book. The reader’s imagination takes flight. It costs the traveler nothing because our imagination is without limit. There are magical places around the world. Take your pick. The shrouded mystery of Machu Picchu, musical Vienna, the opulence of Venice, history frozen in time in Pompeii. Great as these are, there are wonders close to home. Old Sacramento is one of them, and it’s less than two hours away. The entire area has witnessed a rebirth that is extraordinary. The level of excitement is high, but the downside is the incredible noise pollution. Tourists are delighted at every turn, but the noise from the street is deafening. Take yourself back in time for dinner on the refurbished paddle-wheeler Delta King. You can really have some fun here if you “dress for dinner” and make a big entrance into the oak-paneled dining room. Not far from old town is the Crocker Art Gallery. They used to present concerts in the old days before Covid. Let’s hope the concerts will resume. It’s worth the drive. At the opposite end of Old Town is the railroad museum, a Time Machine of unique stature. All the docents bring history to life. They even have “the Gold Spike.” Learn how the Transcontinental railroad was built; combining the political genius of Abraham Lincoln, some incredible graft and corruption, the triumph over racial prejudice, manifest destiny, and much more. There is considerable romance to train travel. Get into the mood by listening to the whimsical humor of Rossini’s The Little Pleasure Train and the flights of fantasy in Jaume Torrent’s Journey to a Magic World. Torrent promises to play it the next time he is in Piedmont. Two composers were able to capture the actual sounds of trains in music. Heitor Villa-Lobos did it in his Little Train of the Caipira. Arthur Honegger did it in his Pacific 231, which should be seen in the 1949 movie with vintage trains. For lighter fare I recommend Roy Clark singing Folsom Prison Blues or Hank Williams singing his own Ramblin’ Man. All aboard! One of the posters in Old Town Sacramento urging Californians to vote the California way. It reminds me of the way they used to vote in Chicago – vote early and often.

articles.text: The Legion of Honor, one of the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco, has opened an exhibit entitled Color into Line: Pastels from the Renaissance to the Present, which will be on display through February 13, 2022. Color into Line displays 80 masterpieces created with pastels from the Renaissance era to modern day. Featured artists include Edgar Degas, muralist Diego Rivera, John Altoon, Wayne Thiebaud and Joan Mitchell, as well as rarely-displayed artworks. The exhibition draws from the archival works of the Achenbach Foundation for Graphic Arts, as well as selected loans from local private collections. Tickets may be purchased by visiting https://legionof honor. famsf.org/exhibitions/pastels. Diego Rivera is a featured artist at the current Color into Line exhibit at the Legion of Honor in San Francisco.

articles.text: The Oakland Museum of California (OMCA) will present an exhibition celebrating Edith Heath, designer and founder of Heath Ceramics, beginning November 13. Edith Heath: A Life in Clay showcases the legacy of the artist with over 50 pieces of ceramics, clay samples, photographs, and personal memorabilia on display. A documentary video will be shown inside the museum as well. The new exhibition introduces visitors to the artist’s career, which was deeply expressive of California’s land and lifestyle. Heath, who died in 2005, focused on creating dependable and long-lasting products for the home, with a focus on sustainability. A Life in Clay is organized by OMCA Curator of Photography Drew Johnson, and guest curator Jennifer Volland. The exhibition will be on display through June 2022. “Edith Heath transformed our notion of ‘good design’ pioneering a new aesthetic of natural, stylish yet functional products made from local materials and designed to endure,” said Johnson. “As an icon of quintessential California design who lived and worked in Sausalito and San Francisco, OMCA is excited to share the extraordinary story of Heath’s life and legacy.” A Life in Clay examines Heath’s technical experimentations with native California clays and glaze formulas. Her love of natural landscapes shaped the quality of her design and inspired her to seek clays from California rather than what was traditionally used for dinnerware. “What began as a rebellion against imported white clay more than 50 years ago is now a modern-day classic,” explained Volland, who has researched the artist since 2014 and served as an essayist for the book Edith Heath: Philosophies. To learn more about the exhibition, and to purchase tickets, visit www.museumca.org. Photo courtesy of UC Berkeley Edith Heath, founder of Heath Ceramics
articles.title: Oakland Museum exhibition of Heath Ceramics founder opens Nov. 13

articles.text: UC Berkeley’s Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive (BAMPFA) currently is showcasing the work of celebrated Japanese cinematographer Kazuo Miyagawa in a series that continues through November 28. Miyagawa (1908-1999) is the visual stylist behind classic films directed by Akira Kurosawa, Kenji Mizoguchi, and Koa Ichikawa, among others. The best examples of his stylistic work and videography will be shown, several of which are in the film archive’s collection. Rashomon, Sansho the Bailiff, and Ugetsu will be shown, as well as other scope-format masterpieces. “Longtime BAMPFA filmgoers may remember Miyagawa’s March 1981 visit, a time [when] he was still actively making films and spoke about his development as a young filmmaker,” said Susan Oxtoby, Director of Film and Senior Film Curator. “A firm believer in filmmaking as a collaborative art form, Miyagawa felt it worked best when a director allowed space for a cinematographer or actors to bring their own creativity to the interpretation of the script.” To learn more, and to purchase tickets for screenings, visit https://bampfa.org/program/ kazuo-miyagawa-cinematographer-and-visual-stylist.
articles.title: Pacific Film Archive screening films on Kazuo Miyagawa through Nov 28

Take yourself back in time for dinner on the refurbished paddle-wheeler Delta King. You can really have some fun here if you “dress for dinner” and make a big entrance into the oak-paneled dining room. Not far from old town is the Crocker Art Gallery. They used to present concerts in the old days before Covid. Let’s hope the concerts will resume. It’s worth the drive. At the opposite end of Old Town is the railroad museum, a Time Machine of unique stature. All the docents bring history to life. They even have “the Gold Spike.” Learn how the Transcontinental railroad was built; combining the political genius of Abraham Lincoln, some incredible graft and corruption, the triumph over racial prejudice, manifest destiny, and much more. There is considerable romance to train travel. Get into the mood by listening to the whimsical humor of Rossini’s The Little Pleasure Train and the flights of fantasy in Jaume Torrent’s Journey to a Magic World. Torrent promises to play it the next time he is in Piedmont. Two composers were able to capture the actual sounds of trains in music. Heitor Villa-Lobos did it in his Little Train of the Caipira. Arthur Honegger did it in his Pacific 231, which should be seen in the 1949 movie with vintage trains. For lighter fare I recommend Roy Clark singing Folsom Prison Blues or Hank Williams singing his own Ramblin’ Man. All aboard! Oakland Museum exhibition of Heath Ceramics founder opens Nov. 13 By Allyson Aleksey The Oakland Museum of California (OMCA) will present an exhibition celebrating Edith Heath, designer and founder of Heath Ceramics, beginning November 13. Edith Heath: A Life in Clay showcases the legacy of the artist with over 50 pieces of ceramics, clay samples, photographs, and personal memorabilia on display. A documentary video will be shown inside the museum as well. The new exhibition introduces visitors to the artist’s career, which was deeply expressive of California’s land and lifestyle. Heath, who died in 2005, focused on creating dependable and long-lasting products for the home, with a focus on sustainability. A Life in Clay is organized by OMCA Curator of Photography Drew Johnson, and guest curator Jennifer Volland. The exhibition will be on display through June 2022. “Edith Heath transformed our notion of ‘good design’ pioneering a new aesthetic of natural, stylish yet functional products made from local materials and designed to endure,” said Johnson. “As an icon of quintessential California design who lived and worked in Sausalito and San Francisco, OMCA is excited to share the extraordinary story of Heath’s life and legacy.” A Life in Clay examines Heath’s technical experimentations with native California clays and glaze formulas. Her love of natural landscapes shaped the quality of her design and inspired her to seek clays from California rather than what was traditionally used for dinnerware. “What began as a rebellion against imported white clay more than 50 years ago is now a modern-day classic,” explained Volland, who has researched the artist since 2014 and served as an essayist for the book Edith Heath: Philosophies. To learn more about the exhibition, and to purchase tickets, visit www.museumca.org. One of the posters in Old Town Sacramento urging Californians to vote the California way. Miyagawa (1908-1999) is the visual stylist behind classic films directed by Akira Kurosawa, Kenji Mizoguchi, and Koa Ichikawa, among others. The best examples of his stylistic work and videography will be shown, several of which are in the film archive’s collection. Rashomon, Sansho the Bailiff, and Ugetsu will be shown, as well as other scope-format masterpieces. “Longtime BAMPFA filmgoers may remember Miyagawa’s March 1981 visit, a time [when] he was still actively making films and spoke about his development as a young filmmaker,” said Susan Oxtoby, Director of Film and Senior Film Curator. “A firm believer in filmmaking as a collaborative art form, Miyagawa felt it worked best when a director allowed space for a cinematographer or actors to bring their own creativity to the interpretation of the script.” To learn more, and to purchase tickets for screenings, visit https://bampfa.org/program/ kazuo-miyagawa-cinematographer-and-visual-stylist.

articles.text: Mary and Bill Geong attend a ceremonial gala in Washington D.C. honoring Chinese American World War II veterans. Piedmont resident Bill Geong received the Congressional Gold Medal on behalf of his father who served the nation during World War II. A ceremonial gala was held in Washington D.C. on September 30 honoring Chinese American World War II veterans and their families. The medal is a bronze duplicate of the Congressional Gold Medal awarded to veterans in recognition of their service. It is estimated that 20,000 Chinese Americans served in the Armed Forces during World War II, and that 40% of those who served were not citizens due to laws that denied citizenship to persons of Chinese descent. In December 2018 a bill was signed recognizing the military services of Chinese Americans despite facing discrimination in the country they served. “It was a bitter-sweet moment for us because, my father-in-law missed the occasion by a year,” said Mary Geong, wife of Bill Geong. “The Japanese American World War II veterans were awarded this honor [years prior] and the Filipinos who fought alongside American GIs in World War II were honored in 2017. It is fitting that the Chinese American veterans finally received recognition for their services in 2018,” she said. In 2019, the Piedmont City Council issued a proclamation honoring Chinese American veterans. The proclamation was presented to members of the Piedmont Asian American Club on April 1, 2019. “Although small in numbers, Chinese Americans made important contributions to the World War II effort,” explained Geong. “They are widely acknowledged for their role in the 14th Air Force, widely known as the Flying Tigers. Additionally, many Chinese American women served in the Women’s Army Corps, the Army Air Forces, and the United States Naval Reserve Women’s Reserve. Some became pilots, air traffic controllers, flight trainers, weather forecasters, occupational therapists, and nurses.” The obverse design depicts Chinese American servicemen and a nurse, representing the service branches in World War II. The reverse design features an Iowa class battleship, an M4 Sherman tank, and a P-40 Warhawk from the Flying Tigers in front of an American flag from the 1940s. The U.S. Mint produced one 24-carat gold medal, valued at $70,000, which is permanently displayed in the Smithsonian National History Museum.

The City’s Sustainability Division wants feedback and all residents are invited to share their input and suggestions through an online community survey. We anticipate that the survey will take 10-20 minutes to complete. All questions are optional, and your responses will remain anonymous. The survey will be available until Friday, November 26. Your responses will shape the EV priorities and actions the community will take in the coming years to address climate change. The City of Piedmont’s Climate Action Plan 2.0 provides a roadmap for reducing greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions in the community. By Allyson Aleksey Piedmont resident Bill Geong received the Congressional Gold Medal on behalf of his father who served the nation during World War II. A ceremonial gala was held in Washington D.C. on September 30 honoring Chinese American World War II veterans and their families. The medal is a bronze duplicate of the Congressional Gold Medal awarded to veterans in recognition of their service. It is estimated that 20,000 Chinese Americans served in the Armed Forces during World War II, and that 40% of those who served were not citizens due to laws that denied citizenship to persons of Chinese descent. In December 2018 a bill was signed recognizing the military services of Chinese Americans despite facing discrimination in the country they served. “It was a bitter-sweet moment for us because, my father-in-law missed the occasion by a year,” said Mary Geong, wife of Bill Geong. “The Japanese American World War II veterans were awarded this honor [years prior] and the Filipinos who fought alongside American GIs in World War II were honored in 2017. It is fitting that the Chinese American veterans finally received recognition for their services in 2018,” she said. In 2019, the Piedmont City Council issued a proclamation honoring Chinese American veterans. The proclamation was presented to members of the Piedmont Asian American Club on April 1, 2019. “Although small in numbers, Chinese Americans made important contributions to the World War II effort,” explained Geong. “They are widely acknowledged for their role in the 14th Air Force, widely known as the Flying Tigers. Additionally, many Chinese American women served in the Women’s Army Corps, the Army Air Forces, and the United States Naval Reserve Women’s Reserve. Some became pilots, air traffic controllers, flight trainers, weather forecasters, occupational therapists, and nurses.” The obverse design depicts Chinese American servicemen and a nurse, representing the service branches in World War II. The reverse design features an Iowa class battleship, an M4 Sherman tank, and a P-40 Warhawk from the Flying Tigers in front of an American flag from the 1940s. The U.S. Mint produced one 24-carat gold medal, valued at $70,000, which is permanently displayed in the Smithsonian National History Museum. articles.text: A large group of walkers received a guided tour of Millionaires’ Row at Mountain View Cemetery last Wednessday, October 27. The Walking on Wednesdays group had a special Halloween week tour of the Mountain View Cemetery on Wednesday, October 27. A strong turnout of 40 participants met in front of the cemetery’s main mausoleum and were led on a guided tour by long-time cemetery docent Jane Leroe, a 75-year old groundbreaking trial attorney. Jane explained that in the early 1860s a group of leading local businessman led by Samuel Merritt, a San Francisco physician and also the 13th mayor of Oakland from 1867 to 1869, created the cemetery under the California Rural Cemetery Act of 1859. His group bought 200 acres of fields far from the center of Oakland for the cemetery so that it would always be in a rural setting. Mountain View was established in 1863 and 26 acres were added later. A total of 170,000 people are buried there with space for an equal number in future years. It was designed by Frederick Law Olmsted, the landscape architect who also designed New York City’s Central Park and much of UC Berkeley and Stanford University. The association that the founders formed still operates the cemetery today. Many of California’s most important historical figures are buried at Mountain View. Including Hearst Castle architect Julia Morgan, Alexander and Josephine Dunsmuir of Dunsmuir House, Anthony Chabot of Chabot Observatory, railroad tycoon Charles Crocker, Domingo Ghirardelli of Ghirardelli Chocolate, Oakland mayor Samuel Crockett, and the “Black Dahlia” Elizabeth Short. One of the cemetery’s main attractions is “Millionaires’ Row,” a section where the most grand, elaborate crypts stand, housing some of California’s most famous and wealthy residents. It is located at the peak of a hill with an expansive view of Oakland, the Bay, and San Francisco. Jane noted that these businessmen came to California around 1850, and were the men who sold the miners the things they needed. At the time the cemetery was created, Egyptian archeological discoveries were being made by the western world, and everything Egyptian was the rage. The cemetery’s Egyptian obelisks and pyramids reflect that popularity. There are two tiers of Millionaires’ Row. The lower tier was for the wealthy, and the upper tier was for the really wealthy. The tomb of Samuel Merritt is Jane’s favorite because of all the beneficial things he did and created for the area. Locals realized it was Merritt who was responsible for the lake in the middle of Oakland, so they simply referred to it as “Lake Merritt.” The walkers were then told the history of Charles Crocker, Domingo Ghirardelli, “Borax” Smith, Charles Doe of UC Berkeley Library fame, and many others. The walkers found Jane to be an animated storyteller, providing candor and humor to give life to these long dead people. Before leaving, Jane told a final story of the Grand Army of the Republic soldiers’ graveyard. They were Civil War Union veterans who died in California, or whose bodies were moved to Mountain View. You may have most of the ingredients on hand, and it only takes about 30 minutes to prepare. Along with garlic, Spanish pimentón de la vera dulce is the flavor forward ingredient here. It originates from the Extremadura/La Vera region of Spain, where the mild, red peppers are dried over oak fire. It adds a warm, smokey note to everything from soup and stews to dry-rubs and even breading/ coating mixes. It’s in frequent use in my kitchen, but I still store it in the refrigerator to ensure it retains its bright flavor. Given that this soup is of modest nature, it is easy to embellish. Add minced red bell pepper whilst sautéing the onions and garlic and add a diced tomato when you add the broth. But take care to not embellish so much that the garlicy-ness becomes muted. Spanish-Style Garlic Bread Soup Adapted from The New Spanish Table by Anya von Bremzen Serves 4 Ingredients • 1/4 cup extra-virgin olive oil, plus additional as needed • 1/2 medium yellow onion, finely diced • 12 cloves garlic, about 1/4 cup, minced. Set aside 1 tablespoon of the garlic to use in the 2nd addition of garlic to the soup • 2 ounces Serrano ham, finely diced. Substitute with prosciutto. • 6 ounces bread, cut into 1-inch cubes. Use batard, round loaf, or baguette. Dayold bread is ideal. • 2 teaspoons sweet, smoked Spanish paprika, pimentón de la vera dulce • 4 cups chicken broth or stock Instructions 1. Heat the olive oil in a heavy 4-quart saucepan over low heat. Add the onions and most of the garlic (reserving the 1 tablespoon to add later), and ham, stirring until the onion becomes translucent and the garlic is very fragrant, about 4 – 5 minutes. Do not let the onion or garlic take on any browning. 2. Add the cubes of bread and stir to coat the bread evenly with the oil, about 2 - 3 minutes. Add a bit more oil if needed. 3. Remove the pan from the heat and sprinkle in the paprika. Stir to coat the cubes of bread evenly. Return the pan to the burner and add the chicken stock. Increase the heat to medium and simmer for about 5 minutes. You want to bread to expand but retain its shape. Add the reserved 1 tablespoon of minced garlic and cook another minute or so. Taste and adjust seasoning. 4. To poach the eggs: Crack one egg into a small ramekin. Make a small well in the simmering soup and carefully pour out the egg into the prepared well. Repeat with remaining three eggs then cover the saucepan. Let the eggs poach in the simmering soup undisturbed for about 5 minutes until the whites are set and the yolks reach the desired consistency. (I prefer the yolks to be slightly runny, which when stirred into the soup add a velvety texture.) 5. Carefully ladle the soup into serving bowls, adding the poached egg last so it floats on top. Garnish with parsley and serve immediately. For more information and to suggest a food to be reviewed, see the blog of Piedmont resident and cook Deborah Quok: PiedmontPantry.com.

articles.text: An American White pelican with large fishhooks lodged into its throat and fishing line encircling its neck and bill succumbed to injuries on October 31, despite being rescued from Lake Merritt on Wednesday and treated by the Oakland Zoo. After receiving fluids, and food at the Zoo’s Veterinarian hospital the pelican, nicknamed Merritt, was transferred to the International Bird Rescue where she passed away. Using two kayaks and a small motorboat to reach and then catch the pelican, Oakland Zoo’s VP of Animal Care, Colleen Kinzley, and Zoological Manager Andrea Dougall, brought the bird to Oakland Zoo’s Veterinary Hospital for treatment. Upon arrival at the Zoo, veterinary staff examined the bird, administered fluids, conducted a blood draw, and checked the injured area on the neck. From initial observations, they determined that the fishing tackle had prevented the bird from being able to eat or drink for weeks, and was suffering from dehydration, starvation, and possible anemia. The staff fed Merritt smelt and capelin fish and had early hopes for her recovery. Her death serves as a vivid reminder of the dangers of fishing items left in Lake Merritt and in all waterways. “Untold numbers of birds, turtles and other wildlife are affected by this solvable issue. Proper disposal of fishing line is crucial, and every citizen can help by picking up any fishing items found in nature,” said Amy Gotliffe, Vice President of Conservation at Oakland Zoo. An American White pelican, named Merritt, was ensnared by multiple barbed hooks on a fishing lure. Between 2002 and 2015, a study by the Audubon Society reported that California-based International Bird Rescue treated at least 2,957 birds for injuries caused by fishing gear. The Oakland Zoo urges guests and the public to join them in Taking Action for Wildlife by changing fishing habits to help save birds and other marine life like Merritt the pelican. When fishing, never leave behind lures, hooks, fishing lines, or bait. Dispose of any gear properly in boxes or similar enclosed receptacle within designated disposal areas or at home. A well-known limerick written by Dixon Lanier Merritt, editor of The Tennessean, is often attributed to humorist and poet Ogden Nash: A wonderful bird is the pelican. His bill can hold more than his belican. He can hold in his beak Enough food for a week, But I’m damned if I see how the helican. articles.text: Piedmont resident Bob Fisher died on November 30, 2020 at the age of 91. Born Robert Sheldon Fisher in Riverside, CA, he gained an appreciation for classical music at a young age thanks to a grade school teacher and listening to radio broadcasts of the Metropolitan Opera in New York City on Saturdays. As a child he also developed a life-long love of trains and was an avid model railroader throughout his life. He enjoyed multi-generational trips to the Redwood Valley Railway in Berkeley’s Tilden Park with his sons, grandsons and great-grandsons, and on occasion with all four. As a philosophy major at the University of California at Berkeley, he began attending performances of San Francisco Symphony and San Francisco Opera, something he enjoyed until his last years. Bob was a long-time board member of the Wagner Society of Northern California, and went with them to Bayreuth, Germany to see Wagner’s Ring cycle. He was editor of the Wagner Society’s quarterly newsletter for over 20 years, and transformed it into a well-respected scholarly journal, Leitmotive, with international subscribers. Bob’s musical knowledge and passion for opera was appreciated by his many friends at both San Francisco Symphony and San Francisco Opera. A highlight of his year was speaking with Maestro Herbert Blomstedt backstage during Blomstedt’s annual conducting trip to San Francisco. Bob was also a long time board member of The College Preparatory School in Oakland, ranked in 2007 by the Wall Street Journal as the sixth best high school in the United States. While chairman of the board of trustees, he led the acquisition of a new site and the construction of a new campus, which opened in 1983 and doubled the student capacity. All three of Bob’s sons graduated from College Prep. Bob was a fixture at the annual Piedmont Fourth of July parade and could frequently be seen at Piedmont High School sports events cheering on his local grandsons. He loved to treat his grandsons to baseball games, the opera and the symphony. Bob built and lived in his delightful, cozy Piedmont home for over 40 years. He was loved and respected by friends and neighbors for his charm, intelligence and kindness. Bob Fisher is survived by sons Benjamin (Margaret), Thomas (Marina), and Seeger, as well as six grandsons, Winston, Matthew (Emily), Myles (Lindsay), Benjamin Jr. (Grace), Edward, and Mitchell. He is additionally survived by three great-grandchildren, Dennis, Robert and Clara. He is predeceased by sisters Olive Steinen and Jean Bohr. A memorial will be held on November 6, 2021 at 1:15 p.m. at Mountain View Cemetery, 5000 Piedmont Avenue, Oakland. In lieu of flowers, memorial donations may be made to The Salvation Army or San Francisco Symphony. Bob Fisher died on November 30, 2020 at age 91. After graduating from UC Berkeley in 1951, Bob married Ann Gordon Clise of Seattle. Their three sons, Ben, Tom and Seeger, all grew up in Berkeley along with a succession of wellloved golden retrievers. Bob was a 2nd Lieutenant in the U.S. Army in the Korean War from 1952 to 1953. After returning home, he opened Berkeley’s first high-fidelity store, The Audio Shop. In 1955 he started a new business, Fisher Berkeley Corporation, which manufactured nurse-call and doctor-locator communication systems for hospitals nationally and internationally. He served as the chief executive officer for over 40 years before selling the business in 1998 upon his retirement. Bob’s loyalty to his employees was demonstrated annually through a carefully selected Christmas present, given to each of his employees in Berkeley, meticulously wrapped by Bob and his family.

articles.text: Bonnie Stehr, who truly valued family and friendships above all else, passed away on October 11, 2021 at the age of 78. Bonnie took great pride in the accomplishments of her family, creating memories through a lifetime of summers at Lake Tahoe. She enjoyed every opportunity she had with her vast directory of friends that spanned classmates, business associates, and community members. She possessed a wonderful, endearing, and fun-loving spirit. She was always enthusiastic and eager to contribute, support and assist. She was an exemplary mother, grandmother, sibling and friend. Born in San Francisco, she was the daughter of Fred and Jean Drewes. She grew up in Piedmont and attended Piedmont High School. She went on to graduate from U.C. Berkeley where she was a proud alumnus and active member of the Pi Beta Phi sorority. Bonnie married her high school sweetheart, Jim, and eventually settled in Piedmont. A renowned cook, Bonnie leveraged her culinary skills to form Bonnie’s Cooking. Following her divorce from Jim, Bonnie embarked on an extremely successful 30-year career as an Account Manager with healthcare benefits company Sitzmann, Morris and Lavis. Following her retirement, she settled in her townhome in Hiller Highlands where she hosted or participated in numerous warm gatherings that included her multitude of friends and family. She thoroughly enjoyed travel, Cal and Stanford sports, and reveled in Town and Country Club events. Regardless of the activity, Bonnie had the ability to maintain a tremendous degree of positive energy that had a tangible effect on many. Her boundless Bonnie Stehr died on October 11, 2021 at age 78. capacity for love had her always willing to open her heart to others. She will be deeply missed by many. Bonnie is survived by her sons, Jim (wife Danya) and Michael (wife Maryanne), her 3 brothers, Michael (wife Barbara), John (wife Susette) and Doug, and her five grandchildren, Bennett, Clayton, Emily, Peter and Jack.

articles.text: The 34th annual Piedmont Avenue Halloween Parade, organized by merchants on Piedmont Avenue, returned this year to a large crowd of families dressed for the occasion on Saturday morning, October 30. This year, due to countywide restrictions from the COVID pandemic, all activities took place outdoors. The Avenue was closed for about three hours for a costume parade and trick-ortreating. With Piedmont Grocery owner Dave Larson as Grand Marshal, the parade was led by bagpiper Fred Payne, beginning at Pet Food Express on Piedmont Avenue and Montell Street. Piedmont Avenue Elementary School’s trunk-or-treat supported the parent-teacher association and Friends of Piedmont Library organized an arts and crafts table for young parade attendees at Key Route Plaza. One of the highlights of the event was the pet costume contest, hosted by Pet Food Express, which awarded gift card prizes for best dressed dog. Valerie Ow Lee, co-owner of J. Miller Flowers, participated as a judge at the event. “I have loved dogs my entire life and always used to dress up my Jack Russell, Rosie, for all of her 19 years. It was enjoyable to search for the cutest, most clever and fun Halloween costumes for pets in our area,” she said. “The experience is pure joy, to see our community come alive with Dog Costume Contest judges at Pet Food Express with the winner, a Whippet in his “Ruff Seas” costume. smiles, costumes, pets and merriment is just icing on the cake.” The parade on Piedmont Avenue has been a tradition for decades, and is uniquely special to the merchants. “The parade builds so much community and goodwill. It shows that together our small businesses support and appreciate our loyal clients and customers,” Ow Lee said. “Families were eager to be outside, dress up in silly costumes and trick-or-treat for candy. They surely missed the Halloween and pumpkin fun last year. We provided a safe and fun community venue on Piedmont Ave - it was so well received, and people can’t wait to attend next year.” Larson echoed Ow Lee’s sentiments when reflecting on the parade’s resonance with merchants and neighbors of Piedmont Avenue. “I think the parade is a great thing for Piedmont Avenue and a great way to connect with the community,” Larson said. The parade was started in 1986 by a number of merchants who wanted to give kids a safe place to trick-or-treat. Richard Stone, the late owner of Continental Hearing and a member of the Lions’ Club, used the opportunity to raise money for Children’s Hospital and the Lions Center for the Blind in Oakland. articles.text: In the late 1950s when Khrushchev denounced Stalin, there was a softening to the West and the forbidden modern art masterpieces began to emerge. Moscow’s Pushkin Museum and Leningrad’s (St. Petersburg) Hermitage took over one of the greatest collections of modern masters in the world. Natalya Semenova curated both the Shchukin exhibition and the Morozov exhibition She began with very little media, only two portraits and a photograph, plus access to interview a Morozov great-grandson living in Paris. She spent five years piecing together the Morozov story by digging into French and Russian archives, bills of sale, jottings and notes, memoirs, and letters. The Morozov family has received no compensation for their lost art. Already a blockbuster, the Morozov exhibit starts at the galleries below ground, and zigzags to all four levels. On the day we attended, the crowds overflowed, and the queues were long, as it was a Saturday. The exhibit runs through February 22. Louis-Vuitton Foundation’s ultra-modern cultural center with its warren of galleries, terraces, and outlooks, rises from the thickly vegetated Bois du Boulogne, a winged splendor of translucent glass against massive, exposed wood and steel beams. The views are spectacular. Madame Forsyth and Michael Mathews, the Piedmont Post’s Americans in Paris, are enjoying autumn in Paris during a typically rainy season. Sure-footed boots and a brawly are recommended. Send comments to: pkf.empower@gmail.com. “La Mer aux Saintes-Maries”, by Vincent Van Gogh, 1888
